selection_basis: Twenty distinct historical cases with reported criminal findings; five modern research priorities selected for documentation, analytical tractability, and public relevance. This is not a ranking of guilt or a comprehensive screen of all organizations.

cases.name: Bernard Madoff / BLMIS
cases.focus: Investment statements versus independently confirmed assets
cases.outcome: Madoff received a 150-year sentence after pleading guilty to operating a Ponzi scheme.
cases.lesson: Independent custody confirmation matters more than a smooth reported return series.

cases.name: Allen Stanford / Stanford International Bank
cases.focus: Deposit backing and independent asset confirmation
cases.outcome: Stanford was sentenced to 110 years following a jury conviction involving fraudulent certificates of deposit and misappropriated investor funds.
cases.lesson: Claims about investment backing require evidence independent of the promoter.

cases.name: Tom Petters / Petters Company
cases.focus: Purported merchandise purchases and resale documentation
cases.outcome: Petters was convicted of fraud-related offenses and sentenced in April 2010 to 50 years; the DOJ describes fabricated merchandise transactions.

source.title: DOJ: Operation Broken Trust in action

cases.lesson: Match purported transactions to independent buyers, goods, and settlement evidence.

cases.name: Scott Rothstein / RRA
cases.focus: Existence of purported confidential settlements
cases.outcome: Rothstein received a 50-year sentence after guilty pleas involving a Ponzi scheme and bogus settlement investments.
cases.lesson: Confidentiality claims do not substitute for independent verification of a receivable.

cases.name: Sam Bankman-Fried / FTX
cases.focus: Customer liabilities versus available customer assets
cases.outcome: Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years after conviction for fraud and conspiracy involving FTX customer funds.
cases.lesson: Reconcile customer claims to independently verified assets and related-party transfers.

cases.name: Elizabeth Holmes / Theranos investor fraud
cases.focus: Investor claims versus independent technical validation
cases.outcome: Holmes was sentenced to 135 months for defrauding investors. This entry concerns the investor-fraud convictions, not all allegations made in her trial.

source.title: DOJ: Elizabeth Holmes sentenced for defrauding investors

cases.lesson: Technical claims need external validation; commercial enthusiasm is not validation.

cases.name: Jeffrey Skilling / Enron
cases.focus: Reported performance and financial reporting
cases.outcome: Skilling was resentenced to 168 months for fraud and conspiracy. This records the revised sentence rather than the original sentence.

source.title: DOJ: Former Enron CEO Skilling resentenced

cases.lesson: Cash-versus-earnings differences are screening questions; establish the accounting mechanics separately.

cases.name: Bernard Ebbers / WorldCom
cases.focus: Financial reporting and accounting manipulation
cases.outcome: A jury convicted Ebbers in the WorldCom fraud case. The entry records the conviction, not his later sentence or custody status.

source.title: DOJ: Statement on the Bernard Ebbers conviction

cases.lesson: Model accounting adjustments with their supporting journal entries, not ratios alone.

cases.name: Dennis Kozlowski and Mark Swartz / Tyco
cases.focus: Corporate benefits, approvals, and executive transfers
cases.outcome: A New York court opinion records Kozlowski and Swartz's grand-larceny convictions. Other people named in the civil opinion are not labeled convicted by this entry.

source.title: New York court: Levin v Kozlowski, 2006 NY Slip Op 52142(U)
source.publisher: New York State Law Reporting Bureau

cases.lesson: Separate permitted compensation from transactions lacking appropriate authorization.

cases.name: John and Timothy Rigas / Adelphia
cases.focus: Related entities, co-borrowing, and undisclosed liabilities
cases.outcome: The government brief records securities-fraud convictions and sentences. It also records reversal of one bank-fraud count; the entry does not treat that count as upheld.

source.title: DOJ: Rigas v United States, opposition, No. 07-494

cases.lesson: Consolidate related-party liabilities carefully and retain reversals as counterevidence.

cases.name: Russell Wasendorf Sr. / Peregrine Financial Group
cases.focus: Customer funds and purported bank balances
cases.outcome: The FBI reports Wasendorf's 50-year sentence for a customer-fund fraud involving falsified financial records.
cases.lesson: Obtain confirmations through independent channels rather than contact details supplied by a subject.

cases.name: Phillip Bennett / Refco
cases.focus: Concealed receivables and reporting-window transactions
cases.outcome: Bennett received a 16-year sentence after pleading guilty in the Refco fraud case.
cases.lesson: Compare reporting-date balances with surrounding periods and trace counterparties.

cases.name: Samuel Israel III / Bayou funds
cases.focus: Reported profits and sham independent audit claims
cases.outcome: Israel received a 20-year sentence following guilty pleas; the DOJ describes false financial statements certified by a sham accounting firm.
cases.lesson: Verify auditor independence as well as the financial statement figures.

cases.name: Paul Burks / ZeekRewards
cases.focus: External customer revenue versus investor rewards
cases.outcome: Burks received a 176-month sentence following a jury conviction for operating an Internet Ponzi scheme.
cases.lesson: Distinguish actual external sales from participant deposits and fictional profits.

cases.name: James Merrill / TelexFree
cases.focus: Participant recruitment versus genuine telecom sales
cases.outcome: Merrill received a six-year sentence after pleading guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy in a pyramid scheme disguised as a telecom business.
cases.lesson: A usable product does not establish that participant rewards come from genuine retail demand.

cases.name: Karl Sebastian Greenwood / OneCoin
cases.focus: Cryptocurrency representations versus independently validated functionality
cases.outcome: Greenwood received a 20-year sentence for the OneCoin fraud. The finding in this entry is specific to Greenwood and does not resolve every other defendant's status.
cases.lesson: Validate the claimed technical and economic mechanism independently of marketing material.

cases.name: Glenn Arcaro / BitConnect
cases.focus: Claimed trading income versus investor distributions
cases.outcome: The DOJ case record documents Arcaro's guilty plea to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. This does not label every BitConnect participant guilty.

source.title: DOJ: United States v Glenn Arcaro, case record

cases.lesson: Independently verify trading proceeds before attributing distributions to investment performance.

cases.name: Volkswagen AG / emissions testing
cases.focus: Laboratory results versus ordinary operating conditions
cases.outcome: Volkswagen AG was convicted and sentenced after guilty pleas involving emissions-test cheating, obstruction, and false import statements.
cases.lesson: Test under representative conditions and investigate regime-dependent discrepancies.

cases.name: Martin Shkreli / MSMB securities fraud
cases.focus: Fund performance representations and investor records
cases.outcome: Shkreli received a seven-year sentence following convictions on three securities-fraud-related counts. This entry concerns those convictions, not drug-pricing controversy or all counts tried.
cases.lesson: Reconcile fund performance updates to independent account records and authorized fees.

cases.name: Raj Rajaratnam / Galleon
cases.focus: Repeated pre-announcement trading patterns
cases.outcome: Rajaratnam received an 11-year sentence after conviction on conspiracy and securities-fraud counts involving insider trading.
cases.lesson: Trading anomalies require corroboration about information access; profitable trades alone do not establish insider trading.

cases.name: Amazon Sponsored Ads pricing
cases.status: Public allegations; FTC case page lists pending
cases.focus: Auction pricing transparency
cases.summary: The FTC and states allege undisclosed advertising-auction surcharges. No liability determination is asserted here.
cases.question: Do observed billed auction prices match the rules disclosed to advertisers?
cases.needed_data: Public complaint and disclosed exhibits; reproducible public pricing documentation. Advertiser-level auction logs are not included or presumed public.
cases.method: Document-to-rule comparison; paired auction reconciliation only if open logs become available.
cases.counterevidence: Amazon disputes the allegations and describes relevance and return-on-ad-spend benefits. These claims also require independent verification.
cases.data_gap: No open auction-level ledger is included. No fraud score is computed.

cases.name: Uber One billing and cancellation
cases.status: Public allegations; FTC case page lists pending
cases.focus: Consent, recurring billing, and cancellation
cases.summary: The FTC alleges unauthorized subscription charges and cancellation obstacles; the case page includes amended complaints.
cases.question: Can a reproducible public interface audit verify disclosures and cancellation steps without assuming billing misconduct?
cases.needed_data: Public complaint, interface exhibits, dated public terms. Private user billing logs are outside this dataset.
cases.method: Versioned interface coding and process comparison; pre-register criteria and account for jurisdiction and product version.
cases.counterevidence: The company contests the case. Independent collection of its full response remains incomplete; do not treat the agency's account as the whole record.
cases.data_gap: No open consent or billing event logs; no model-based company conclusion.

cases.name: JustAnswer subscription disclosure
cases.status: Public allegations; FTC case page lists pending
cases.focus: One-off advice expectations versus recurring subscription disclosure
cases.summary: The FTC alleges consumers were enrolled into recurring subscriptions without affirmative consent. The case page records a July 2026 complaint filing.
cases.question: How prominent and consistent are the recurring-charge disclosures across documented versions of the purchase flow?
cases.needed_data: Public complaint and its interface exhibits, public terms, and dated public screenshots with provenance.
cases.method: Blinded disclosure coding with inter-rater agreement; compare equivalent device and purchase-flow versions.
cases.counterevidence: The complete defense record has not been collected. Missing response material is a dataset limitation, not evidence against the company.
cases.data_gap: No open conversion or consumer-consent ground truth; no guilt prediction.

cases.name: LA Fitness membership cancellation
cases.status: Public allegations; June 2026 FTC litigation report records ongoing case
cases.focus: Cancellation accessibility and recurring membership charges
cases.summary: The FTC alleges cancellation obstacles and unwanted recurring charges. This entry does not assert a finding of liability.
cases.question: Do dated public cancellation procedures offer the access described in published terms?
cases.needed_data: Government complaint and exhibits, public terms and dated process descriptions; no private membership records.
cases.method: Process-path comparison stratified by location, agreement type, and time; distinguish recommendation from requirement.
cases.counterevidence: Fitness International has disputed the allegations and described an online cancellation option. The complete defense record has not been independently ingested.
cases.data_gap: No open member-level outcomes. Status is a dated research snapshot, not live court monitoring.

cases.name: Personalized pricing transparency / industry research
cases.status: Public policy study; not a finding of wrongdoing by any named firm
cases.focus: Use of personal data in individualized prices

source.title: FTC: Surveillance pricing update and the work ahead

cases.summary: FTC staff describe initial study insights on data-driven pricing. Public research summaries use hypothetical examples to protect confidential information.
cases.question: Can observed price differences be explained by inventory, geography, timing, or public promotions before attributing them to personal data?
cases.needed_data: Open staff reports, public policy documents, and lawfully collected public price observations. Confidential 6(b) submissions are unavailable.
cases.method: Matched observations or randomized audits where permitted; control for taxes, stock, location, timing, and eligibility.
cases.counterevidence: Different prices can reflect legitimate costs, promotions, or market conditions. A 6(b) study is not a liability finding.
cases.data_gap: No individual-level confidential study data is public; do not manufacture firm-level conclusions.
